title_en: The Author's Introduction — On the Three Classes of the Ummah and the Arrangement of the Nine Stations
arabic_text:
مقدمة المؤلف إن لله سبحاته وتعالى يقول في محكم كتابه يخاطب هذه الأمة المحمدية بكريم ا) قال ابيهقي: قدم الظالملنفسه لكثرة الظالمين لأنفسهم وعقب بالمقتصد لفلة المقتصدين .بالنسبةإلبهم وخر السابق لآن السابقين أهل من القليل. قله الزمخشري. وحكى الطبرسي: أن هذا اترتيب على مقامات الناس؛ فإن أحوال العباد ثللاث: معصية لم اتوبة ثم قربة؛ فإذا عصى العبد فهو ظائم فإذا ثاب فهو مقتصد فإذا صحت تويته وكثرت مجاهدته فهو سابق. .وقيل: قدم الظالم لعلا ييأس من رحمة الله تعالى وأخر السابق لثلا يعجب بعمله قتعين اتوسيط المقتصد. .وقال قطب الدين: التكتة في تفدهم الظالم أن أقرب الثلاثة إلى بداية حال العبد قبل اصطفاه. يايراث الكتاب؛ فإذا باشره الاصطقاء فمن العباد من يتأثر فليا وهو الظالم لنفسه ومتهم من يتأثر تأثزا وسطًا وهو المقتصد ومنهم من يتائر تأثرًا تا وهو السابق. وقريب منه ما قيل: إن الاصطفاء مشكك تتفاوت مراتيه؛ وأولها ما يكون للمؤمن الظالم النفسه وفوقه ما يكون للمقتصد وفوق الفوق ما يكون للسابق بالخيرات فجاء التنيب كالترفي في المراتب. وقيل: أخعل السابق لتعدد ما يتعلق به فلو قدم أو وسط لبعد في الجملة ما بين الأقسام المتعاطفة ولما كان الاتتصاد كالنسبة بين الظلم والسيق اقنضى ذلك تقديم الظالم وتأخير المقتصدا ليكون المقتصد بين الظالم والسابق لقا كما هو يينهما معنى؛ وقد يقال: رتب هذه الثلاثة هذا الترتيب ليوافق حالهم في الذكر بالنسبة إلى ما وعدوا به من الجنات في قوله. سبحانه: ا تمدق الآية حالهم في الحشر عند تحقق الوعد فأخر السابق الداخل في الجنان أولا ليتصل ذكره بذكر الجناث الموعود بها وذكر قبله المقتصد وجعل السابق فاصلا امقدمة المؤلف قال ابن عياس وابن مسعود: (الأصناف الثلائة كلها في هذه الأمة المحمدية: وكلهم في الجنة). وقاله أبو سعيد الخدري.

وقالت عائشة رضي الله عنها: (دخلوا الجنة كلهم)؛ وقال كعب الأحبار: (استوت مناكبهم ورب الكعبة؛ وتفاضلوا بأعمالهم)

وقال أب إسحاق السبيعي: (أما الذي سمعت منذ ستين سنة كلهم ناج).

وقرأ عمر بن الخطاب هذه الآية» ثم قال: قال رسول اله يك: "سَابقَُا سَابقٌء وفص دنا ناوطنا موز 10 له ولا شك أن الراكن لهذا العموم مقرور ما لم يقف سنن الأئمة المهتدين: فقد قال معروف الكرخي: طلب الجنة بلا عمل ذنب من الذنوب» وانتظار الشفاعة بلا سبب نوع من الغروره ورجاء رحمة من لا يطاع حمق وجهل.

وأنا إن شاء الله تعالى أذكر في كتابي هذا أدب هذه الأصناف الثلائة التي ذكرها الله سبحاته؛ وأتكلم عليها في نسعة مقامات بعضها أعلى من بععضء أبدأ بالمقام الناسع؛ ثم أندلى منه إلى المقام الذي بعده إلى المقام الأولء م أثرقى منه إلى المقام الشاني؛ ثم إلى الثالث؛ شم كذلك إلى المقام التاسع» أبدأ به وبه أخنتم؛ خمتم الله لي به بمنه وفضله فأذكر في الشدلي المقصود باختصار» وبالترقي بالبسط والإكثار؛ اقنداء بصاحب كتاب "أدب الدين” الماوردي رضي الله عنهء قال: القلوب ترتاح إلى الفنون ‏ .وذكر حكاية عن المأمون قال: كان يتل في قصره من موضع إلى موضع؛ وينشد قول أبي العتاهية: [البسيط]* ال يصلح النفس إذ كانت مدبرة إلا التتقل من حال إلى حال ينه وبين الجنات؛ لأ إنما يدخلها بعده فيكون فاص بنه وبينها في الدخول وذكر قبلهسا الظالم لنفسه؛ لأنه إنما بدخلها ويتصل بها بعد دخولهما فتأخير السابق في المعنى تقديم وتقديم الظالم في المعنى تأخيرء ويحتمل ذلك أوجها أخرى نظهر بالتأمل فتامل. أروح المعاني: 402/16 (2) تهاية الأرب في فنون الأدب 199/10 اندمة المؤاف 0 وكذلك قول عياض”' في صدر "مداركه": جمعنا من أخبار أعيان المالكية وسير قضاتهم ونوادر من فتاوى فقهائهم ما يحتاج الحكام إليه ولا غنى للعلماء عنه؛ وأثبشا من مناهج صلحائهم ما ترجى بركاته؛ وقد قال سفيان: عند ذكر الصالحين تنزل الرحمة.

وقال أبو حنيفة: الحكايات عن العلماء أحب إل من كثير من الفقه؛ لأنها أدب القوم؛ وانتقيا أثناء ذلك من ملح آدابهم ما ينشط النفس عند كسلهاء ويصقل عنها رين صداتهاء فقد قال علي رضي الله عنه: (سلوا التفوس ساعة وساعة؛ فاتها تصداً. كما يصدأ الحديد).
anchors:
- Root: ظ-ل-م (ẓ-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Placing something in other than its proper position; exceeding the bound (jāwaza al-ḥadd); darkness as a metaphor for deviation from right.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Qur'anic context, ẓālim li-nafsihi denotes the believer who wrongs himself through sin, yet remains within faith — a moral, not metaphysical, injustice.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: transgression of a boundary. Metaphorical (majāz): the soul's own act of self-deprivation of reward — hence "wronging oneself" is figurative, as the soul is not an external victim.
- Root: ق-ص-د (q-ṣ-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To aim at, to take the middle path, to be moderate; the "straight way" (al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm) as the intended course.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The muqtaṣid is the one who balances obedience and repentance — neither excelling in supererogatory works nor persisting in sin.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: intending a destination. Metaphorical: the intermediate rank between excess and deficiency in religious practice.
- Root: س-ب-ق (s-b-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To outstrip, to precede, to be first in reaching a goal.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The sābiq is the foremost in good deeds (sābiq bi-l-khayrāt), one who hastens to obedience and attains nearness (qurbah) to God.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: racing ahead in physical movement. Metaphorical: precedence in spiritual rank and divine favor.
- Root: ص-ف-و (ṣ-f-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To choose, to select the purest part; to clarify (as of honey or cream).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Iṣṭifā' (election) is God's selective favor — graded (mushakkak), varying in intensity across the three classes.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: straining out impurities. Metaphorical: divine election that purifies the chosen from the dross of sin.
- Sībawayh Rule: Al-ʿAṭf wa al-Tartīb (Coordination and Ordering) — In coordinated clauses (al-ʿaṭf bi-thumma), the sequence implies temporal or rank-based succession; the placement of the three nouns (ẓālim, muqtaṣid, sābiq) is governed by semantic gradation, not mere syntax, and the author's reordering (taqdīm/taʾkhīr) is a deliberate rhetorical device (balāghah) requiring exegetical justification.
translation:
The Author's Introduction

I say — and with God is success:

God — glorified and exalted be He — says in the clear verses of His Book, addressing this Muhammadan community with His noble speech: {«ثُمَّ أَوْرَثْنَا الْكِتَابَ الَّذِينَ اصْطَفَيْنَا مِنْ عِبَادِنَا ۖ فَمِنْهُمْ ظَالِمٌ لِّنَفْسِهِ وَمِنْهُم مُّقْتَصِدٌ وَمِنْهُمْ سَابِقٌ بِالْخَيْرَاتِ بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ ۚ ذَٰلِكَ هُوَ الْفَضْلُ الْكَبِيرُ»} [Then We gave the Book as inheritance to those whom We chose from among Our servants: among them is one who wrongs himself, among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who outstrips in good deeds by God's permission — that is the great bounty] (Fāṭir 35:32).

Al-Bayhaqī said: "The one who wrongs himself was mentioned first because of the abundance of those who wrong themselves; the moderate was mentioned second because of the scarcity of the moderate relative to them; and the one who outstrips was placed last because those who outstrip are among the few." Al-Zamakhsharī said the like of this.

Al-Ṭabarsī narrated that this ordering corresponds to the stations (maqāmāt) of people; for the states of the servants are three: disobedience without repentance, then nearness (qurbah); so when the servant disobeys, he is a wronger of himself; when he repents, he is moderate; and when his repentance is sound and his striving (mujāhadah) increases, he is one who outstrips.

And it was said: The wronger was placed first so that he might not despair of God's mercy, and the one who outstrips was placed last so that he might not be amazed by his own deed; thus the moderate was necessarily placed in the middle.

Quṭb al-Dīn said: "The subtle point in placing the wronger first is that he is the closest of the three to the beginning of the servant's state before election (iṣṭifā') to inherit the Book; for when election begins to affect him, some servants are affected weakly — and that is the wronger of himself; some are affected moderately — and that is the moderate; and some are affected strongly — and that is the one who outstrips in good deeds." Near to this is what was said: that election (iṣṭifā') is graded (mushakkak), its degrees varying; its first degree belongs to the believing wronger of himself, above him is the moderate, and above that is the one who outstrips in good deeds — so the mention came as an ascent in ranks.

And it was said: The one who outstrips was placed last because of the multiplicity of what attaches to him; for were he placed first or middle, the distance between the coordinated classes would be excessive in the whole. And since moderation is like the relation between wrongdoing and outstripping, this necessitated placing the wronger first and the moderate last — so that the moderate might be between the wronger and the one who outstrips in mention, just as he is between them in meaning.

And it may be said: These three were arranged in this order to correspond to their state in mention relative to what they were promised of the Gardens in His saying — may He be exalted — {«جَنَّاتُ عَدْنٍ يَدْخُلُونَهَا»} [Gardens of Eden which they enter] — and to their state at the Resurrection when the promise is fulfilled. So the one who outstrips, who enters the Gardens first, was placed last so that his mention might be connected to the mention of the promised Gardens, with him as a link between them and the Gardens; for he only enters after them, and thus he is a separator between them and the Gardens in entry. And the wronger of himself was mentioned before him because he enters and connects to them only after their entry. So the delaying of the one who outstrips is, in meaning, a precedence; and the precedence of the wronger is, in meaning, a delay. And this admits other aspects that appear upon reflection — so reflect.

Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd said: "All three classes are in this Muhammadan community, and all of them are in Paradise." Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī said the same.

ʿĀʾishah — may God be pleased with her — said: "They all entered Paradise." Kaʿb al-Aḥbār said: "Their shoulders are equal, by the Lord of the Kaʿbah; and they differ only by their deeds."

Abū Isḥāq al-Sabīʿī said: "As for what I have heard for sixty years — all of them are saved."

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb recited this verse, then said: "The Messenger of God — may God bless him and grant him peace — said: 'A forerunner is a forerunner, and one who falls short is one who falls short, and the moderate is saved.'"

And there is no doubt that the one who relies on this generality is deluded, so long as he does not stand on the conduct (sunan) of the rightly guided imams. For Maʿrūf al-Karkhī said: "Seeking Paradise without works is a sin among sins; and awaiting intercession without cause is a kind of self-deception; and hoping for the mercy of One who is not obeyed is folly and ignorance."

And I — God willing — shall mention in this book of mine the conduct (adab) of these three classes that God — glorified be He — has mentioned; and I shall treat them in nine stations (maqāmāt), some higher than others. I begin with the ninth station; then I descend from it to the one after it, down to the first station; then I ascend from it to the second; then to the third; and so on to the ninth — I begin with it and with it I conclude. May God seal it for me with His grace and bounty. So I mention in the descent the intended matter with brevity, and in the ascent with expansion and abundance — following the example of the author of the book "Adab al-Dīn," al-Māwardī — may God be pleased with him — who said: "Hearts find rest in variety." And he mentioned a story of al-Maʾmūn, that he would move about in his palace from place to place, reciting the verse of Abū al-ʿAtāhiyah (al-Basīṭ):

"* The soul is not mended, when it is turning away, except by moving from one state to another."

And likewise the saying of ʿIyāḍ at the beginning of his "Madārik": "We have gathered from the reports of the notable Mālikīs, the biographies of their judges, and the rare fatwas of their jurists what judges need and scholars cannot do without; and we have recorded from the ways of their righteous what blessings are hoped for." Sufyān said: "At the mention of the righteous, mercy descends."

Abū Ḥanīfah said: "Stories about the scholars are dearer to me than much jurisprudence (fiqh); for they are the conduct (adab) of the people." And we selected, in the course of that, from the pleasantries of their conduct what revives the soul in its languor and polishes from it the rust of its neglect. For ʿAlī — may God be pleased with him — said: "Give the souls respite hour by hour; for they grow rusty as iron rusts."

anchors:
- Root: ح ك ي (ḥ-k-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To relate, narrate, imitate, or recount an account; the act of transmitting a story or report verbatim.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ḥikāyah denotes the transmission of exemplary narratives (ḥikāyāt al-ṣāliḥīn) as a means of spiritual edification, distinct from formal prophetic narration (riwāyah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — recounting an event; metaphorical (majāz) — the "troops of God" (junūd Allāh) as a simile for the spiritual efficacy of such tales.
- Root: ج ن د (j-n-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: An army, host, or gathered force; troops prepared for battle.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Qur'anic idiom, junūd Allāh refers to God's unseen aids and means of strengthening the faithful, whether material or spiritual.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — armed forces; metaphorical — the spiritual "soldiers" that fortify the hearts of the knowers (ʿārifūn) and the bodies of the aspirants (murīdūn).
- Root: د ل و (d-l-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To lower a bucket into a well; descent toward something; drawing near.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the spiritual path, tadallī signifies the soul's descent from lofty stations to engage with lower realities, while tarqī denotes ascent; together they frame the journey of the seeker.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — lowering a rope; metaphorical — the soul's movement between divine nearness and creaturely engagement.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Inshā' vs. Khabar (Declarative vs. Performative Utterance) — In the author's opening invocation and the reported dialogue, the shift between khabar (informative narration) and inshā' (performative prayer/praise) governs the syntactic structure, requiring the translator to preserve the authorial voice's direct address and supplicatory tone.

And my shaykh, al-Mutaysūrī — may God have mercy on him — related to us by his chain of transmission reaching Abū al-ʿAbbās Ibn al-ʿArīf, who said: I was in the gathering of my teacher Abū ʿAlī al-Ṣadafī, reading ḥadīth before him. One day he read a ḥadīth; then he closed the book and began relating the stories of the righteous (ḥikāyāt al-ṣāliḥīn). It occurred to me: How can the shaykh interrupt the ḥadīth of the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — and relate stories? He said: My thought had not yet settled when the shaykh looked at me askance and said: "O Aḥmad, the stories are troops from among the troops of God (junūd min junūd Allāh) by which God strengthens the hearts of the knowers (ʿārifūn) among His servants." He said: There remained not a single hair on my body but sweat dripped from it. When he saw me bewildered, he said to me: "O Aḥmad, where is the confirmation of that in the Book of God — exalted is He?" I said: "The shaykh knows best." He said: [He then cited the verse] {...} — meaning His saying, exalted: "And We send down of the Qur'an that which is healing and mercy" [al-Isrā' 17:82] — and the verse.

And al-Junayd — may God have mercy on him — said: "The stories are troops from among the troops of God by which God strengthens the bodies of the aspirants (murīdūn)." And my master al-Mutaysūrī — may God have mercy on him — did not cease to delight in relating the accounts of the righteous and in listening to their mention, for in mentioning them mercies descend, and in attending their gatherings their blessings are obtained, and in visiting their graves after their death [there is benefit]. And I have named this book of mine "The Conduct of the Rightly Guided in the Stations of Religion" (Sunan al-Muhtadīn fī Maqāmāt al-Dīn); and it is fitting that it be called "The Descent and the Ascent" (al-Tadallī wa al-Tarqī), for its beginning is a descent and its end is an ascent. And I seek refuge in God — glorified be He — from speaking about knowledge without knowledge, or from acting in religion without certainty. And God suffices me; there is no god but He; upon Him I rely, and He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne. And my success is not but through God; upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn in repentance. And my intention is to follow — even in expression — so I do not exceed the wording of those scholars upon whom I rely.

So I open my book with the praise of Abū Ḥāmid — may God have mercy on him — in his "Iḥyā'": I say: I praise God, my Lord, with a praise [that befits Him], He who made the night and the day a succession for whoever desires to remember or desires gratitude. And may God bless our master Muḥammad, whom He sent with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner.

title_en: The Third Station — On Earnestness in Religion and the Vigilance of the Rightly Guided

anchors:
- Root: ذ-ل-ل (dh-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Submissiveness, tractability; a beast made compliant for riding or burden.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine subjugation of creation to human benefit as a sign of providence (tashkhīr).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal here — the earth's physical tractability; metaphorical extension to the soul's journeying.
- Root: س-ف-ر (s-f-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Uncovering, traveling; a journey as unveiling of new horizons.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The worldly sojourn (safar al-dunyā) as a passage to the abode of recompense.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal travel; metaphorically, the entire human lifespan as a caravan.
- Root: خ-س-ر (kh-s-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Loss, perishing of capital; a deficit in trade.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The eschatological loss (khusrān) of the soul's eternal investment.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal commercial loss; metaphorical for forfeiting the Hereafter.
- Sībawayh Rule: Al-ʿAṭf ʿalā al-Sabab (Coordination on Causal Grounds) — clauses linked by fa- or wa- where the second term is the consequence or counterpart of the first, as in the sequence of journey-stages.
translation:
To proceed: Verily God — exalted be His praise — made the earth submissive (dhulūlan) to His servants, that they might take it as a dwelling, and from it lay up provision, guarding themselves against its snares and its perils; and that they might realize that the lifespan carries them along as a ship carries its passengers. So mankind in this world are but travelers: the first of their way-stations is the cradle, and the last of them is the grave; and the homeland is either Paradise or the Fire. The lifespan is the distance of this journey; the years are its stages; the months are its leagues (farāsikh); the days are its miles; and the breaths are its steps. Obedience is the merchandise; the hours are the capital; the lusts are the highway robbers; and the wind — if it be favorable — is the winning of the encounter with God, exalted be He, in the Abode of Peace, in the company of the Great King and the everlasting bliss. But if it be a loss — God forbid — then it is the forfeiture of this mighty gain. And would that it were only that! Nay, rather, along with it is the painful chastisement in the lowest depths of the Blazing Fire.

So whoever is heedless of a single one of his breaths until it passes away in that which does not bring him near to God as an offering (zulfā), has indeed exposed himself on the Day of Mutual Deceit (yawm al-taghābun) to a ruin and a loss that have no end.

Al-Shāṭibī said in his *Muwāfaqāt*: For this reason, the pious forebears (al-salaf al-ṣāliḥ) subdued their souls under the hardships of devotional exertion. They made equal the obligatory and the supererogatory in seeking the act, and the forbidden and the disliked in seeking abandonment. And they counted whoever did not fill his breaths with obedience as one who had wasted them. Upon this is based the hadith of regret: "On the Day of Resurrection, the doer of good will regret that he did not do more, and the doer of evil will regret that he did not desist." (Reported by al-Tirmidhī, no. 2403; Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in *al-Ishrāf*; al-Bayhaqī in *al-Zuhd*, no. 4716; al-Daylamī in *al-Firdaws*.)

Sahnūn said: I saw Ibn al-Qāsim and others, but I never saw the like of ʿAbd al-Raḥīm. Then it was transmitted from him that he said: Visiting brethren is a diminution of one's works. And from the sayings of Sahnūn: Look always at two matters in both of which there is reward; the heavier of them upon you is the more excellent.

قبل لسهل بن عبد الله النستري”؛ منى يستريح الفقير؟ قال: إذا لم بر غير الوقت الذي هو فيه.

وحدئتسي شيخي المتتوري عن جدي ابسن بقي عن شيخه الأستاذ المقري»
anchors:
- Root: ث ق ل (th-q-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Heaviness, weightiness; that which burdens the soul and weighs upon the heart.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The heavier act (al-athqal) is that which most opposes caprice (hawā) and thus most purifies intention (ikhlāṣ) in obedience.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical weight; metaphorical: moral and spiritual gravity — the act whose performance is most arduous to the lower self (nafs).
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional precedence (taqdīm al-sharṭ) — the protasis (law istaqāma) governs the apodosis, requiring the reader to hold both alternatives in suspense until the resolution.
translation:
Al-Muḥāsibī said: “Begin with God’s commands according to the most obligatory, then the next most obligatory, and the most excellent, then the next most excellent. If it does not become clear to you which of two matters is more excellent and more obligatory, then undertake that which is heavier upon your heart — for you cannot be secure that, in performing the act which is light upon you, you are not acting from your own caprice (hawā) rather than for your Lord, Glorified be He. If the two matters become equal, and you are unable to discern which of them is heavier or lighter, then let the servant present himself, at that very moment, before death — as if he were already established upon it — and ask: upon which of the two would he love for death to overtake him? For the believing soul, even if it be heedless and disobedient, does not wish for the meeting with God, nor love it, except upon that [state] which is the pure good (al-khayr al-ṣāfī) that it hopes will deliver it from the punishment of God, Glorified be He — because at death it has no caprice in this world; its caprice in this world is only for life, so long as it remains living.”

Abū Ḥāmid said: “Every breath of yours is a seal (khātima), for it is possible that death may be joined to it. Consider: even if it is not the final breath, the masters of the hearts have said: ‘There is no breath you exhale but that it has a decree (qadar) in you which it executes, and a judgment (ḥukm) which it fulfills.’ It is incumbent upon you to direct that breath toward obedience to your Master, and to be content with what comes to you from Him, even if it opposes your caprice. For if you defer this breath to another breath, this breath will pass away, and regret will overtake you for it.”

Tāj al-Dīn said: “Do not await the completion of external distractions (firāgh al-aghyār), for that will cut you off from the reality of vigilance (murāqaba) over God in that which He has established you in.” And he said: “Your deferring of deeds until the existence of leisure is from the follies of the souls (raʿūnāt al-nufūs).”

And consider this alongside what they have said: that Sufism (taṣawwuf) is to be in the present moment (al-waqt), in that which is most appropriate for the moment.

It was said to Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Tustarī: “When does the poor one (al-faqīr) find rest?” He said: “When he sees nothing other than the moment in which he is.”

And my shaykh al-Mattūrī related to me, from my grandfather Ibn Baqī, from his shaykh, the teacher al-Maqqarī…

وقال أبو حامد: اتقاء مواضع الخلاف مهم في الورع في حق المفتي والمقلد فإذا أفتى المقلد إمامه بشيء ولإمامه فيه مخالف؛ فالفرار من الخلاف إلى الإجماع. من الورع المذكور.

وقال محبي الدين النووي”'': أهل العلم متفقون على الحث على الخروج من الخلاف إذا لم يلزم منه إخلال بسنة؛ قال أبو مصعب*: كان مالك”' يطيل السجود والركوع في ورده؛ وإذا وقف في الصلاة كأنه. أصابه ما أصابه قيل له: لو خففت من هذا قليلاء قال: لا ينبغي أن يعمل عملا ل إلا حسته قال تعالى: يوسيعلا [الملك: 2]. الى يابسة ل يتحرك منه شيء: فلما (ا) هو: يحبى بن شرف؛ محبي الدين: أبو زكريا النووي؛ كبير الفقهاء في زماته؛ كان من الزهاد. مولدء ووفات بتوى؛ من قرى حوران: قرأ النحو على ابن مالك وغيره. صنف: شرح مسلم» ورياض الصالحين؛ والأذكار؛ وتهذيب الأسماء واللغات, والمجموع شوح المهذب ولم يتمه. توفي سنة 676ل ترجمته في: تذكرة الحفاظ 70/4)
anchors:
- Root: ج-د-د (j-d-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "newness" and "freshness," but in the sense of jidd (with kasrah) it denotes earnestness, seriousness, and vigor in undertaking a matter—the opposite of laxity or jest (hazl).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the theological context, jidd signifies the soul's firm resolve (ʿazm) in pursuing acts of obedience to Allah, untainted by worldly complacency or concession-seeking; it is the operative virtue of the muḥtadī (rightly guided one) in the stations of religion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, jidd is the "freshness" of effort; metaphorically (majāz), it is the intensification of one's striving in worship and legal rigor, as opposed to rukhṣah (concession), which is a lesser degree of the same root.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — When the author juxtaposes "al-jidd" with "al-dīn," the genitive construction (iḍāfah) binds them syntactically, indicating that earnestness is not an accessory but an intrinsic property of the religion itself, as parsed in the nominal sentence structure.
translation:
I say—and Allah grants success—

Know that among the exemplars of earnestness in religion is the account of Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh al-Iskandarī (d. 709 AH / 1309 CE). He was Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Karīm, Abū al-Faḍl, Tāj al-Dīn Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh al-Iskandarī: a Shādhilī Sufi and a scholar. He was among the most vehement opponents of Ibn Taymiyyah. Among his works are: al-Ḥikam al-ʿAṭāʾiyyah (printed) on spiritual refinement; Unwān al-Tawfīq (printed) on exhortations and admonitions; and Laṭāʾif al-Minan fī Manāqib al-Mursī wa Abī al-Ḥasan (printed). He died in Cairo. The book Miftāḥ al-Falāḥ is attributed to him, but it is not of his authorship. See: al-Durar al-Kāminah 1:273, al-Riḥlah al-ʿAyyāshiyyah 1:357, Kashf al-Ẓunūn 675, Khiṭaṭ Mubārak 6:9, and his death year is recorded as 787, and Brockelmann in the Encyclopaedia of Islam 1:200, and Muʿjam al-Maṭbūʿāt 2:184.

And Sahl al-Tustarī (200–283 AH / 815–896 CE): Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yūnus al-Tustarī, Abū Muḥammad: one of the imams of the Sufis, their scholars, and those who discoursed on the nullification of insincerity (ikhlāṣ), spiritual exercises (riyāḍāt), and the defects of deeds. He authored a book on (Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm, printed, abridged), and the book Ruqaq al-Muḥibbīn, among others. [From al-Aʿlām 3:143, he said verbatim: "The reality (ḥaqīqah) is: a people acting upon the precedents (sawābiq) and apportioned according to the consequents (lawāḥiq); and the Sufi is one who has no past—if you are its glass, then good for you."]

And Tāj al-Dīn said in his "Ḥikam": "The rights of the moments (ḥuqūq al-awqāt) cannot be made up (qaḍāʾ), for there is no moment that arrives except that Allah has upon you in it a new right and a confirmed command; so how can you fulfill therein the right of another while you have not yet fulfilled the right of Allah in it?"

I say: ʿIyāḍ reported that Mālik was never seen by any of his family or friends except wearing a turban, dressed in his garments, not laughing, and not speaking about what did not concern him. And he would say: "A scholar is not truly a scholar until he is thus—and until he exercises precaution (iḥtiyāṭ) for himself in matters that, were he to abandon them, he would bear no sin therein."

And Ibn al-Qāsim narrated from him that he said: "Ziyād would place his hand on my shoulder and say: 'Upon you is earnestness (al-jidd); for if what your companions say regarding concessions (rukhaṣ) is true, it will not harm you; but if the matter is otherwise, then you have indeed taken hold of earnestness.'"

I say: Ibn Rushd said: "Ziyād urged Mālik to adopt for himself, in his private affairs, the most stringent of what has been said regarding ijtihād in the rulings of religion. For the mujtahid who has perfected the tools of ijtihād is obligated in his private affairs to follow what he sees by his own ijtihād, not what another sees by his ijtihād if it is more lenient. This is among the matters that are recommended for him, upon what Ziyād urged upon Mālik in this anecdote." This ends the quotation from Ibn Rushd.

And Abū Ḥāmid said: "Avoiding the loci of disagreement (khilāf) is important in scrupulousness (waraʿ) for both the muftī and the muqallid. So when the muqallid's imam issues a fatwā on something, and the imam has an opponent therein, then fleeing from disagreement to consensus (ijmāʿ) is part of the aforementioned scrupulousness."

And Muḥyī al-Dīn al-Nawawī said: "The people of knowledge are in agreement on urging the exit from disagreement (al-khurūj min al-khilāf) when it does not entail a violation of a Sunnah."

I say: Abū Muṣʿab said: "Mālik would lengthen the prostration and the bowing in his regular devotional prayers (wird); and when he stood in prayer, it was as if something had afflicted him. It was said to him: 'Would you lighten this a little?' He said: 'It is not fitting that one perform an act except with excellence (iḥsān).' Allah Most High said: {«الَّذِي خَلَقَ الْمَوْتَ وَالْحَيَاةَ لِيَبْلُوَكُمْ أَيُّكُمْ أَحْسَنُ عَمَلًا»} [al-Mulk: 2] — 'He who created death and life to test you which of you is best in deed.' He would remain until his feet became dry, not a part of him moving."

title_en: On the Station of Sincerity in Religion and the Balance Between Rigor and Leniency
arabic_text:
209 - 2781 (2) ملف هو: أبو مصعب مطرف بن عبد لله بن مطرف بن سليمان ين يسار اليساري الهلالي ابن أخت الإمام مالك - رحمه اله - من رجال الطبقة الوسطى من تلاميذ مالك؛ تفقه به ويكبار تلامذته: مثل: عبد المالك بن الماجشون وابن كتانة والمغيرة... أخوج له البخاري في الصحيح... قال الإمام أحمد - رحمه الله -: كانوا يقدمونه على أصحاب مالك. ولد - رحمه الله - سنة 139 ها وتوفي سنة 226 بالمدينة فيما ذكرهالاام البفاري. انظر؛ ترتيب المدارك 133/3 - 135.

(3) مو مالك بن أنس بن مالك الأصبحي: أب عد له المدني؛ وإمام دار الهجرة صاحب الموطأً. والمذعب المعروف. توفي سنة 179 أحد الأمة الأربعة المجتهدين: الذين هم أبو حنيفة: ومالك؛ والشافمي وأحمد أصحاب المذاهب الأريعة وهناك مذاهب لأهل السئة؛ لكن اتقرضت؛ مثل: مذهب سفيان الثوري؛ ومذهب ابن جرير الطبري. فمالك هو أحد الأنم الأربعة المقنّدين؛ وهو إمام جليل؛ يسمى يإمام دار الهجرة ‏ يعني: المدبنة-؛ ويسمى عالم المدينة؛ واشتهر في وقنه؛ حتى قيل؛ ل يقنى ومالك في المدينة وذلك لعظيم منزلته وثقة الثأس به؛ رحمه لله رحمة واسعة.

- 1474: وطيقات الشافعية الكبرى 395/8 - 400: والبداية.

انظر هذا الذي كان عليه مالك من الجد في الدين؛ وما أجمع عليه العلماء من اتقاء مواضع الخلاف: ومراعاة الأنفاس مع الله وإيثار الأثقل على النفس والأفضلء الذي لو فجأء الموت وهو عليه ما وجد أفضل منه؛ ولا يود أن يلقى لله إلا عليه كما قاله سحنون وغيره؛ هو الحق الذي لا شك فيه؛ فمن ذم ما دون هذا المقام أو قال: إنه من لهو الحديث؛ أو قال: بدعة؛ فماذا بعد الحق إلا الضلال بالنسبة لهذا بة إضافية ولا سيما وربما لا يكون هو في هذا المقام؛ فذلك حبجة عليه ومذعب لبهاء أقاويل العم اء في الآبة الشريفة التي افتتحت بها كتابي.

ومن شأن العلماء به وباحكام لله أن يذهبوا مع الناس في الرخصة والسعة ما الم يخف المأئم. صح من 'التمهيدا”

ومن "الرسالة": كان رويم'' من جملة المشايخ مقرثًا فقيهاء قال: من حكم الحاكم أن يوسع على إخوانه في الأحكام؛ ويضيق على نفسه فيهاء فإن التوسعة اتباع العلم والتضييق على نفسك من حكم الورع. وسيأتي أن المرء لا يأخذ على أهله بالورع؛ فإن كان ما ذم لم ينه الله عنه ولا نبيه؛ ولا اتفق الناس على ال فسيأتي في المقام السادس أنه لا إثم على مرتكبه؛ وإن كنا نقول: إن مرتكبه ظالم النفسه؛ ولا نقول: إنه ضال مبندع وقل أنت: إنه ظالم لنفسه؛ كما تقول عن نفسك: اللهم إن كنت في الوقت مما هو أولى في الوقت فلله درك؛ وما أظنك لو كنث إلا وغبت عن الأغيار إلا جهاد الكفار؛ تقول بلسان حالك ونطفك ومقالك: 9وَحَجلتُ تن 47 [له: 81].

الما ذكر الإمام مربي المريدين البلالي”' ثمرات المحبة؛ قال: ومنها نظر غير (1) رويم بن أحمد بن يزيد بن رويم: صوفي شهيرء من جلة مشايخ بغداد توفي 330ه من كلامه: (الصبر ترك الشكوى: والرضا استلذاذ البلوى). انظر: الأعلام 37/3.

(2) البلالي: محمد بن علي بن جعفر البلالي شمس الدين العجلوني الشافمي الصوفي زيل مصير ولد سنة 750 وتوفي سنة 812 اثني عشرة وثمانماثة. صنف السول في أحاديث الرسول. مختصر أحياء العلوم للغزالي. [هدية العارفين 41/2] منهج النالي/ الما النابع: الأ بالجد في الدين هه الكفرة بعين الرحمة؛ فمن فقد هذه العلامات كذب في دعوى المحبة. وأما قولك: ضال أو مبتدع؛ فتفول على الشارع. وكان سيدي ابن سراج”' رحمه الله يرشح هذا القول؛ ويقول: هذه هي بدعة الضلالة؛ أعني: أن تحكم على الشيء بغير حكمه» وسيأني لعز الدين” في المقام الثالث أن: من الكذب على الله أن يلحق المكروه بالحرام.

انظر بهذا الملحظ الاستلقاء لا كان. ولكن لما وردت الأحاديث الصحيحة بالنهي عنه.

ورد أيضًا أن رسول الله كه استلقى رشح مالك هذا الخير بفعل الخلفاء أنهم استلقوا تحريًا أن لا يظن في الاستلقاء أنه مكروه: قال أبو عمر”: أتى مالك بفعل الخلفاء. ولو لم يرد عنهم أنهم استلقوا لكان الأصل الإباحة؛ لآن الأحاديث إذا تعارضت ولم يعلم الناسخ من المنسوخ تساقطت؛ ويبقى الشيء على إياحته' إذ لا يثبت حكم على مسلم إلا بدليل لا معارض له.
anchors:
- Root: ج-د (j-h-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Exertion of effort to the utmost; striving with seriousness and resolve.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Religious striving (ijtihād) in worship and knowledge; the earnest pursuit of divine command.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in physical effort; metaphorical in spiritual diligence and moral rigor.
- Root: و-س-ع (w-s-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Amplitude, spaciousness; capacity to encompass.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine leniency (rukhṣah) in legal dispensations; the breadth of permissible action.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical breadth; metaphorical for legal and ethical latitude.
- Root: ر-خ-ص (r-kh-ṣ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Softness and ease; a concession after hardship.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Legal dispensation granted by the Lawgiver in exceptional circumstances.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for tender flesh; metaphorical for jurisprudential easing.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — Governing the nuanced parsing of "if... then..." and "except..." clauses to preserve the author's precise legal qualifications.
translation:
I say — and success is from God alone:

Know that the biography of Abū Muṣʿab al-Hilālī, the nephew of Imām Mālik — may God have mercy on him — is recorded among the middle stratum of Mālik's students. He studied jurisprudence under him, and among his eminent disciples were ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Mājishūn, Ibn Kinānah, and al-Mughīrah. Al-Bukhārī included him in his Ṣaḥīḥ. Imām Aḥmad — may God have mercy on him — said: "They used to give him precedence over the companions of Mālik." He was born in the year 139 AH and died in the year 226 in Medina, as al-Bukhārī mentioned. See: Tartīb al-Madārik, 3/133–135.

As for Mālik ibn Anas al-Aṣbaḥī — the Imām of Medina, the Imām of the Abode of Hijrah, author of al-Muwaṭṭaʾ, and founder of the well-known school — he died in the year 179. He is one of the four mujtahid Imāms of the nation: Abū Ḥanīfah, Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Aḥmad, the founders of the four schools of the People of the Sunnah. There were other schools among the Ahl al-Sunnah, but they became extinct, such as the school of Sufyān al-Thawrī and that of Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī. Thus Mālik is one of the four authoritative Imāms; he is a venerable leader, called "Imām of the Abode of Hijrah" — meaning Medina — and "the Scholar of Medina." He became renowned in his time, to the extent that it was said: "No one gives legal verdicts while Mālik is in Medina," due to his immense station and the people's firm trust in him. May God have mercy on him with abundant mercy.

See: Ṭabaqāt al-Shāfiʿiyyah al-Kubrā, 8/395–400, and al-Bidāyah.

Now, reflect upon what Mālik was upon — the earnestness in religion, the consensus of the scholars on avoiding points of disagreement, the mindfulness of one's breaths with God, and the preference for what is heavier upon the soul and more excellent — such that if death were to come upon him suddenly while in that state, he would find nothing better, and he would not wish to meet God except upon it, as Saḥnūn and others have said. This is the truth about which there is no doubt. Whoever disparages anything below this station, or says it is "idle talk," or calls it "innovation" — then what is there after truth except error? This applies relative to that station, especially since perhaps the critic himself is not upon it. Thus it is an argument against him and a refutation of his claim, according to the words of the scholars concerning the noble verse with which I opened my book.

It is the way of the scholars — those who know God and His rulings — to go with the people in concession (rukhṣah) and latitude (saʿah) as long as no sin is feared. This is established authentically in al-Tamhīd.

And from al-Risālah: Ruwaym — may God have mercy on him — was among the eminent shaykhs, a jurist. He said: "It is part of the judge's wisdom to be expansive toward his brethren in rulings, and to be strict upon himself therein; for expansion is following knowledge, and strictness upon oneself is a matter of scrupulous piety (waraʿ)." It will come later that a man is not to impose scrupulous piety upon his family. For if what is criticized is not forbidden by God or His Prophet, nor is there consensus upon its prohibition — then it will come in the sixth station that there is no sin upon its practitioner. Although we say: its practitioner is unjust to himself, we do not say: he is misguided or an innovator. Rather, say: "He is unjust to himself," just as you say of yourself: "O God, if I am in a time [of weakness], then what is more fitting for the time — may God reward you." And I do not think that if you were [truly sincere], you would be absent from others except in striving against the disbelievers. You say with the tongue of your state, your utterance, and your speech: {وَحَجَلْتُ} [Q. 47:81] — "And I was veiled."

The Imām, the mentor of seekers, al-Bilālī — may God have mercy on him — mentioned the fruits of love. He said: "Among them is looking upon the creature with the eye of mercy." Whoever lacks these signs has lied in his claim of love. As for your saying "misguided" or "innovator" — that is speaking against the Lawgiver. My master Ibn Sirāj — may God have mercy on him — used to endorse this statement and say: "This is the innovation of misguidance — namely, that you judge a thing by other than its proper judgment." And ʿIzz al-Dīn will come in the third station to state: "Among the lies against God is attaching the disliked (makrūh) to the forbidden (ḥarām)."

Consider this point of reflection. For when the authentic ḥadīths prohibiting reclining [while drinking] were reported, the prohibition was established. But it is also reported that the Messenger of God ﷺ reclined. Mālik endorsed this good practice by the action of the caliphs — that they reclined, deliberately, lest reclining be thought disliked. Abū ʿUmar said: "Mālik cited the action of the caliphs." And had it not been reported that they reclined, the original principle would be permissibility (ibāḥah). For when ḥadīths conflict and the abrogating cannot be distinguished from the abrogated, they cancel each other out, and the matter remains upon its original permissibility — since no ruling is established against a Muslim except by an evidence that has no countervailing proof.

title_en: On Matters Resembling Lying Down (Istiqlā') in Rulings: Disagreement, Permissibility, and the Principle of Default Permissibility

وقال ابن العربي*' في "مسالكه" لما ذكر الاستلقاء والنهي عنه قال ما نصه؛ (!) محمد الغرناطي (844ه - 1444م) محمد بن محمد بن سراج الأنالسي؛ الغرناطي (أبو القاسم) ققبء من الفضاة مشارك في علوم: من تصايفه: شرح كيير على ممختصر خليل في فروع الققه المالكي.   * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The literal sense is physical posture; the metaphorical extension here is the *ruling-pattern* (ma'nā ḥukmī) — i.e., any act whose licitness is debated among jurists, thus transferred from the physical to the normative domain.

  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A worldly (dunyawī) act whose permissibility is established by Prophetic tacit approval (taqrīr), thus a model for acts of play and leisure.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: dancing. Metaphorical: any act of permissible recreation that the strict-minded might deem improper, but which the Law (Sharʿ) has effectively sanctioned.

  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: joking. Metaphorical: the "salt" of social intercourse — permissible in measure, like salt in food.

  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Taʿziyah (التعزية) — condolence, consoling the bereaved; from ʿazā' meaning patience and consolation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A communal act of mercy; its permissibility toward non-Muslims (ahl al-dhimmah) is affirmed by Mālik and Sahnūn, distinguishing it from love (mawaddah), which is prohibited.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: comforting. Metaphorical: the juristic distinction between permissible courtesy (birr) and forbidden affection (mawaddah) — a nuance of intent, not merely action.

translation:
I say — and Ibn al-ʿArabī (may God have mercy on him) said in his "Masālik" when he mentioned lying down (al-istiqlā') and the prohibition against it, stating verbatim:

The conflicting ḥadīths [on this matter] — their ruling is that they cancel each other out, and one returns to the foundational principle; and the foundational principle is permissibility (al-ibāḥah) until a prohibition arrives, and no ruling is established against a Muslim except by an evidence that has no opposing counterpart.

End of his quote.

And consider here a secondary branch (farʿ) whose ruling resembles the ruling of lying down — namely, that when the statements of the scholars conflict concerning a matter, some saying it is prescribed (mashrūʿ) and others saying it is not prescribed, then I say: never is this [disputed matter] lower in rank than the permissible (mubāḥ). Rather, those whose religion and trustworthiness I rely upon among the Mālikī and Shāfiʿī imams have stated explicitly: whatever some imams have deemed disliked (makrūh) and others have deemed recommended (mustaḥabb), then performing it is more virtuous — such as raising the hands [in prayer] — because the Sacred Law is cautious on behalf of performing the recommended acts, just as it is cautious on behalf of performing the obligatory acts.

And what those whom I trust in their religion among the Mālikīs and Shāfiʿīs have mentioned regarding this matter is a point of disagreement [among them], and I shall clarify this, God willing.

And consider also what is even lower [in rank] than lying down, upon whose permissibility the scholars have also explicitly ruled — namely, dancing (al-zafn). ʿIyāḍ said: "Al-zafn is dancing. ʿUmar feared that it might be something improper, so he pelted the Abyssinians with pebbles because of it. But the Prophet (peace be upon him) rebuked him and said to them: 'Carry on...' — the ḥadīth." ʿIyāḍ said: "In this is the strongest evidence for its permissibility, for the Prophet (peace be upon him) added to their continuance [by his tacit approval] and even encouraged them."

End of the quote from "al-Ikmāl."

And from this same meaning is jesting (al-mizāḥ) — they explicitly ruled on its permissibility, and ʿIzz al-Dīn [Ibn ʿAbd al-Salām] restricted it to what does not terrify the soul, does not pain the heart, and the like — as stated by Imām al-Māwardī. And he recited:

"Give your weary nature, worn by earnestness, some rest — and season it with a measure of jest. But if you give it jest, let it be in the measure that food is given of salt."

And consider also, from this same meaning, offering condolence (al-taʿziyah) to the people of the dhimmah — the scholars feared that it might be thought improper, so they explicitly stated that it falls under the category of the permissible. And al-Qarāfī devoted a distinction (farq) between it and love (al-mawaddah).

[Al-Qarāfī said:] "And that courtesy (al-birr) is permissible, unlike love." Mālik said: "A man may offer condolence to his non-Muslim neighbor for the death of his non-Muslim father, due to the covenant of neighborliness (dhimām al-jiwār). He may say: 'I have been informed of what befell you in the loss of your father; may God join him with the great of his religion and the best of his community.'" And Sahnūn said: "He may say to him: 'May God compensate you for your misfortune, and reward you with the best of what He has rewarded anyone among his people.'"

And in the marginal notes (ṭurrar) of Ibn ʿĀt: "There is no harm in attending the wedding feast of a Jew and eating from it."

And some of our companions [said] — after administering an oath to him by the Torah that he had not married his paternal aunt nor his maternal aunt.
